headline: High-risk shared filesystem and git writes make prompt injection, data leakage, and cascading errors plausible by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Both agents can read and write files, and Agent A explicitly shares state with other instances via filesystem and git, while Agent B uses a mounted volume. That creates a default content bridge where attacker-controlled files from either side can be treated as instructions. No provenance or isolation is documented.
conditions: IF either agent reads instructions from shared files without provenance checks
IF a shared workspace or mounted volume contains attacker-controlled content
mitigations: Separate the agents onto distinct workspaces
Disable shared mounted volumes between runtimes
Add a manual review step before either agent consumes files from the other
Use provenance tags for any cross-agent file handoff
requires-engineering: enforce content filtering on shared files

B_data_leakage.rationale: Agent A touches source code, cwd files, and shell environment; Agent B touches files mounted into its runtime. Because both have broad network egress and filesystem access, sensitive material placed in a shared workspace can flow into either agent’s outputs or upstream APIs. The profiles do not show default encryption or isolation beyond separate runtimes.
conditions: IF sensitive files are mounted into both runtimes
IF either agent forwards file contents to its model backend or MCP server
mitigations: Keep secrets out of shared directories
Mount only the minimum required files into each runtime
Rotate API keys after any shared-workspace session
Review outbound network destinations before use
requires-engineering: add DLP controls on mounted volumes

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Both agents can write the filesystem and modify git state, and Agent A shares state via filesystem and git while Agent B shares via mounted volume. In a shared repo, concurrent edits and git operations can overwrite each other or corrupt history. No locking or coordination primitive is documented, so the conflict is dangerous by default.
conditions: IF both agents operate on the same repository or mounted workspace
IF either agent performs git commits, rebases, or file rewrites concurrently
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate branch
Pause one agent before the other writes
Use a lock file around git operations
Review diffs before merging
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level concurrency control

D_cascading_error.rationale: Agent A can emit shell and file outputs that Agent B may consume, and both support MCP and broad tool use. If B treats A’s artifacts as authoritative, a mistaken command, patch, or fact can cascade into further edits or actions. The profiles show no built-in verification step between them, so the failure chain is plausible in default use.
conditions: IF Agent B consumes Agent A’s output as input without verification
IF Agent A produces a patch, command, or factual claim that B executes or renders
mitigations: Require human review before B acts on A’s output
Add a verification prompt between agents
Limit A to drafting only, not execution
Log and diff all handoffs
requires-engineering: implement schema-validated handoff contracts

E_compliance.rationale: Both profiles are open-source and do not state a residency, certification, or retention mismatch. The only clear compliance concern is that Agent A handles a Google API key and Agent B handles model-provider API keys, so mishandling secrets could create policy issues, but the pairwise compliance gap is not documented. The other agent is cited because the risk is about the pair’s shared handling of secrets.
conditions: IF regulated data is placed into either runtime
IF secret-handling policies differ between the two deployments
mitigations: Keep regulated data out of both runtimes
Store secrets in a dedicated vault
Confirm retention settings before use
Document which runtime may see which data class
requires-engineering: align compliance controls across deployments
